overview_paragraphs: SAP ECC to Salesforce migrations are among the most common cross-platform data movements in enterprise IT. They typically occur when companies are modernizing their customer-facing operations — moving away from SAP's tightly coupled ERP model toward Salesforce's cloud-native CRM for sales, service, and marketing. This migration is often triggered by M&A activity, digital transformation initiatives, or the desire to give commercial teams a purpose-built CRM instead of forcing them into SAP's customer management modules.

The technical complexity is significant. SAP ECC stores customer and partner data across deeply normalized structures — KNA1 (general data), KNVV (sales area data), KNVP (partner functions), and KNVK (contact persons) — while Salesforce uses a flatter object model with Accounts, Contacts, and Opportunities. Custom fields, SAP number ranges, partner function hierarchies, and sales organization-specific data all need to be untangled and remapped. Currency and unit-of-measure conversions, SAP-specific date formats (YYYYMMDD), and industry-specific configurations add further complexity.

Most companies handle this migration through consulting engagements that rely on manual field mapping in spreadsheets and custom ABAP or middleware-based ETL. This approach typically takes 6–12 months, costs $1–3M, and requires deep SAP functional knowledge that's increasingly hard to find.

Salesforce doesn't have a native equivalent — these relationships typically need to be modeled using Account hierarchies, custom junction objects, or Salesforce's Contact Roles. The mapping decision affects downstream process design.

overview_paragraphs: SAP ECC to S/4HANA is the defining enterprise migration of this decade. With SAP ending mainstream ECC maintenance in 2027, virtually every SAP customer is planning or executing this transition. It's also one of the most technically demanding migrations in enterprise IT — not because the source and target are different products, but because S/4HANA fundamentally restructures how SAP stores data.

The core challenge is S/4HANA's data model simplification. Hundreds of ECC tables have been merged, renamed, or eliminated. The MATDOC table replaces MKPF/MSEG for material documents. The ACDOCA universal journal replaces dozens of FI/CO line item tables. The Business Partner (BP) model replaces separate customer (KNA1) and vendor (LFA1) masters. Every custom Z-table, report, and interface that touches these structures needs to be analyzed and potentially rewritten.

Consulting firms typically quote 12–24 months and $5–20M for a brownfield S/4HANA migration. The data conversion workstream alone — profiling custom objects, mapping to simplified structures, validating referential integrity across the new data model — consumes 30–40% of the program budget.

overview_paragraphs: Dynamics GP to Dynamics 365 is one of Microsoft's most heavily promoted upgrade paths, and for good reason — GP has been in maintenance mode since Microsoft shifted investment to D365 Finance & Operations and Business Central. Companies on GP face dwindling support options, an aging Dexterity-based architecture, and an inability to integrate with modern cloud services. The migration is often timed with hardware refresh cycles or driven by the need for real-time reporting and API-based integrations that GP cannot provide.

Despite both being Microsoft products, the data architectures are fundamentally different. GP uses a proprietary Dexterity-based SQL Server schema with non-intuitive table names (RM00101 for customers, PM00200 for vendors, SOP10100 for sales orders) and a flat, wide-table design. Dynamics 365 uses the Dataverse entity model (for Business Central / CE) or normalized X++ data entities (for Finance & Operations). The chart of accounts structure changes significantly — Cloud uses a tree-based segment hierarchy instead of EBS's value sets. Setup data (payment terms, tax codes, units of measure) must be recreated in Cloud before transaction data can load.

Oracle offers the Cloud Migration Toolkit, but it covers only a subset of data objects and assumes a relatively vanilla EBS installation. Companies with extensive customizations — which is most enterprise EBS deployments — face significant manual effort mapping DFFs, custom tables, and modified workflows to Cloud equivalents.

Generating correctly formatted FBDI files from EBS data requires precise transformation logic and loading sequences that respect cross-object dependencies.

challenges.title: Descriptive Flexfield (DFF) and global segment conversion

Oracle Cloud has its own DFF framework with different context structures and naming. Each EBS DFF context-segment combination must be mapped to the equivalent Cloud DFF or replaced with a Cloud extensible flexfield — and the data values converted accordingly.

challenges.title: Chart of accounts restructuring for Cloud segments
challenges.description: EBS uses accounting flexfield value sets with independent or dependent validation. Oracle Cloud uses tree-based hierarchies for each COA segment. The value set-to-tree conversion is non-trivial — parent-child relationships must be explicitly defined in Cloud's tree structure, and cross-validation rules must be recreated as Cloud segment rules.

challenges.title: Setup data migration before transaction data
challenges.description: Oracle Cloud requires all reference data (payment terms, tax codes, currencies, UOM, supplier sites, customer sites) to be loaded and validated before any transaction data can import. The sequencing is strict — a single missing setup record causes entire FBDI loads to fail. Identifying the complete setup data dependency tree from EBS is a project in itself.

overview_paragraphs: Legacy database to Salesforce migrations are among the most varied and unpredictable migration types. The source could be anything — a Microsoft Access database that's been running for 15 years, a custom SQL Server or MySQL application, a FoxPro system, a FileMaker database, or even flat files exported from a decommissioned mainframe. These migrations are triggered when companies finally replace homegrown or legacy CRM systems with Salesforce, often as part of a broader digital transformation or after an acquisition where the acquired company has no standard CRM.

The core technical challenge is that legacy databases have no standard schema. Unlike migrating from SAP or Oracle where the table structures are known, a custom database requires discovery from scratch — table relationships must be inferred from foreign keys (if they exist), data types are often inconsistent, business logic lives in application code rather than the database, and there's rarely documentation. Field naming conventions are unpredictable, and the same conceptual entity (a customer) might be spread across multiple tables with no obvious join path.

Companies typically handle these migrations with brute-force manual effort — a database developer exports tables to CSV, a Salesforce admin manually maps columns to Salesforce fields, and someone spends weeks fixing data quality issues one field at a time. For large legacy databases with 50–200 tables, this process takes 4–8 months.

challenges.title: Undocumented schema discovery

Mine's schema profiler infers relationships from data patterns — matching column values across tables to discover implicit joins.

challenges.title: Inconsistent data types and encoding
challenges.description: Legacy databases often store dates as strings, phone numbers as integers, booleans as Y/N or 1/0 or T/F, and currencies without decimal precision. Character encoding may vary between tables (Latin-1, Windows-1252, UTF-8). Every field needs content analysis, not just schema analysis, to determine the correct Salesforce target type.

challenges.title: No standard object model

A 'Customers' table might combine what Salesforce separates into Accounts, Contacts, and Leads. A 'Transactions' table might contain sales orders, invoices, and payments mixed together with a type column. Decomposing these composite structures into Salesforce's object model requires business logic decisions.

challenges.title: Data quality issues accumulated over decades
challenges.description: Legacy databases accumulate data quality issues over their lifetime — duplicate records created by different application versions, orphaned foreign keys from deleted records, truncated fields from past schema changes, and test data mixed with production data. These issues aren't just migration problems — they need to be resolved before data enters Salesforce.

bridge_paragraph: Dynamics GP uses a proprietary Dexterity-based SQL Server schema with non-descriptive table names — RM00101 for customers, PM00200 for vendors, GL00100 for accounts — while NetSuite uses a modern cloud-native entity model with intuitive record types. Mine translates GP's legacy naming conventions and flat table structures into NetSuite's subsidiary-based dimensional model automatically.
overview_paragraphs: Dynamics GP to NetSuite migrations happen when companies choose NetSuite's cloud-native platform over Microsoft's Dynamics 365 upgrade path. This is common among companies that want a unified ERP/CRM on a single cloud platform, prefer Oracle's infrastructure over Azure, or find NetSuite's mid-market focus better aligned with their complexity level. PE portfolio companies frequently standardize on NetSuite across acquisitions, making GP-to-NetSuite a recurring migration pattern.

The technical challenge combines GP's legacy architecture problems with NetSuite's structural differences. GP's cryptic Dexterity table names (RM00101, PM00200, SOP10100) must be decoded and mapped to NetSuite's entity types. GP's flat chart of accounts needs restructuring into NetSuite's dimensional model with subsidiaries, departments, classes, and locations. Third-party ISV data (Mekorma, Binary Stream, SalesPad) stored in custom tables has no NetSuite equivalent.

Companies typically manage this migration during their NetSuite implementation using CSV exports from GP's SQL database. The table name translation, chart of accounts restructuring, and ISV data handling are largely manual — adding weeks to the implementation timeline.

challenges.title: GP's Dexterity table names to NetSuite entities
challenges.description: GP uses non-descriptive table names inherited from its Dexterity framework — RM00101 (Customer Master), PM00200 (Vendor Master), GL00100 (Account Master), IV00101 (Item Master). NetSuite uses intuitive entity names. Building a complete crosswalk across hundreds of GP tables requires deep knowledge of GP's undocumented schema.

challenges.title: Flat chart of accounts to NetSuite dimensional model
challenges.description: GP uses a flat or minimally segmented chart of accounts. NetSuite uses a multi-dimensional structure with subsidiaries, departments, classes, and locations. Decomposing GP's account structure into NetSuite's dimensional model — and deciding which GP segments become which NetSuite dimensions — requires analysis of actual GL posting patterns.

challenges.title: ISV and third-party module data
challenges.description: Most GP installations include third-party ISV modules (Mekorma for payments, Binary Stream for multi-entity, SalesPad for order management) that store data in custom SQL tables. These have no NetSuite equivalent and require individual analysis to determine migration scope vs. archive vs. rebuild.

challenges.title: Work/Open/History table split
challenges.description: GP stores transactions across separate work, open, and history tables (SOP10100 for sales work, SOP30200 for sales history; GL20000 for open year, GL30000 for GL history). NetSuite uses a unified transaction model. Deciding how much history to migrate and unifying GP's split tables requires careful cutover planning.

overview_paragraphs: Zoho CRM to Salesforce is the classic CRM upgrade migration. This migration is common when companies raise funding and need enterprise-grade CRM, when sales teams scale beyond 50 reps and need advanced territory management, or after M&A events where the acquiring company standardizes on Salesforce.

Despite similar concepts (both have Leads, Contacts, Accounts, Deals/Opportunities), the field-level implementation differs. Zoho's custom modules map to Salesforce custom objects but with different relationship patterns. Zoho's Blueprint automation maps to Salesforce's Process Builder or Flow, but the logic must be rebuilt. Zoho's multi-currency handling, scoring rules, and territory management features have different Salesforce equivalents. Zoho's API field names don't match Salesforce API names even for conceptually identical fields.

Companies typically use Salesforce Data Loader or third-party tools like Import2 or Trujay. The field mapping, picklist alignment, and custom module translation still require significant manual effort — especially for Zoho instances with extensive customization.

challenges.title: Blueprint to Salesforce automation translation

overview_paragraphs: Shopify to NetSuite is the most common ecommerce-to-ERP migration. Shopify Products with Variants map to NetSuite Matrix Items or individual Item records depending on variant complexity. Shopify's customer model is order-centric (customers are often created per order) while NetSuite's is entity-centric. Order data must be restructured from Shopify's flat order model to NetSuite's Sales Order → Invoice → Fulfillment transaction chain. Shopify's discount codes, gift cards, and refund model don't have direct NetSuite equivalents.

Companies typically set up a real-time integration (Celigo, FarApp) for ongoing sync, but the initial historical data migration — products, customers, and order history — still requires a bulk data conversion effort that's often underestimated.

challenges.title: Product variants to NetSuite item structure

challenges.title: Customer deduplication

challenges.title: Order model translation

challenges.title: Discount and pricing model differences

Migrating historical order data with accurate discount representation in NetSuite requires translating Shopify's discount allocations to NetSuite's pricing adjustments.

overview_paragraphs: SugarCRM to Salesforce is a legacy CRM upgrade migration. Companies move from SugarCRM (including SugarCRM Enterprise, Sugar Sell, and older Community Edition deployments) to Salesforce for the ecosystem, AppExchange marketplace, Einstein AI, and the breadth of Salesforce's platform. This migration is common when companies outgrow Sugar's capabilities, when self-hosted Sugar instances become maintenance burdens, or when companies want cloud-native CRM without managing infrastructure.

The migration maps Sugar's module-based architecture to Salesforce's object model. The core concepts are similar — both have Leads, Contacts, Accounts, and Opportunities — but field types, relationship patterns, and customization mechanisms differ. Sugar's Studio customizations (custom fields, layouts, relationships) must be translated to Salesforce's custom fields, page layouts, and Lightning components. Sugar's workflow rules become Salesforce Flows.
Companies typically use Salesforce Data Loader with CSV exports from Sugar's database. The custom module mapping and workflow translation require manual analysis.

Mine catalogs all Sugar workflow and process definitions, documenting field references and trigger conditions for Salesforce Flow rebuilding.

Every legacy HR migration is unique because there's no standard schema. Employee data may be spread across multiple tables with no obvious join path. Job history might be a single 'current job' field with no historical tracking. Pay data might mix salary, hourly, and contractor records in one table. Benefits enrollment might be tracked in spreadsheets entirely outside the database. Mine's value is in the discovery phase — understanding what's in the database before you can map it.

overview_paragraphs: BMC Remedy to ServiceNow is the single largest ITSM platform migration in enterprise IT. Remedy (including Remedy ITSM, Remedy OnDemand, and Helix ITSM) has been the dominant enterprise ITSM platform for decades, but companies are migrating to ServiceNow for its modern cloud architecture, superior user experience, and faster innovation cycles. This migration is driven by Remedy's aging on-premise infrastructure costs, limited SaaS options, and the difficulty of finding Remedy AR System administrators and developers.

The technical complexity is significant because Remedy and ServiceNow use fundamentally different architectures. Remedy stores data in AR System forms — HPD:Help Desk for incidents, CHG:Infrastructure Change for changes, AST:Attributes for CMDB — with custom fields, active links, and escalation rules defined in the AR System. ServiceNow uses relational tables with a different field naming convention, workflow engine, and CMDB structure. Remedy's Atrium CMDB uses a class hierarchy that maps differently to ServiceNow's CMDB class structure.

These migrations are typically managed by large consulting firms over 12–18 months. The data conversion workstream — mapping Remedy forms to ServiceNow tables, translating CMDB class hierarchies, and preserving workflow logic context — consumes 25–35% of the total program effort.

challenges.title: AR System forms to ServiceNow tables

The form-to-table mapping is not one-to-one: Remedy's HPD:Help Desk has different field structures than ServiceNow's incident table. Custom fields on Remedy forms (Character, Diary, Selection, Attachment) must map to ServiceNow field types (String, Journal, Choice, Attachment).

challenges.title: Atrium CMDB to ServiceNow CMDB class hierarchy

ServiceNow's CMDB uses a different class structure (cmdb_ci, cmdb_ci_computer, cmdb_ci_service). The class mapping, CI attribute translation, and relationship type alignment require deep analysis of both CMDB models.

The automation logic doesn't migrate — it must be rebuilt. Mine documents field references and trigger conditions for each Remedy workflow.
